newsitem.title: USA: Photographic silver demand seen up 3 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Photographic silver demand seen up 3 pct in 1997.

text.p: Strong growth in amateur photography will push photographic demand for silver to 233 million ounces this year, up three percent over the 1996 level, according to silver analyst Peter Krause in a mid-year industry outlook released Tuesday by the Silver Institute.
Demand for color film, which increased 11 pct last year, will rise another four pct in 1997, Krause said.
And color photo paper demand, which jumped 17 percent last year, will also increase four percent this year, he said.
"Film consumption for amateur photography got its biggest boost from increased demand in Japan, Russia and China," Krause said.
"Paper volume in this sector benefitted from the continuing shift to larger print sizes and a 17 percent increase in underdeveloped countries."

After amateur photography, the second most important sector for silver demand continues to be medical radiography in which silver-based black and white films are almost exclusively used for image recording and storage.
The use of these materials continues to grow, Krause said, and will increase around three percent annually for at least five years.
"As the population ages, more people will require medical care, and expanding healthcare in developing countries will mean more radiographic services throughout the world," he said.
"These factors will outweigh the trend toward reducing spending per patient due to managed care controls, and the use of electronic systems which are expensive and hard to justify."
But silver consumption in the graphic arts sector is expected to decline by about two percent in 1997.

The main reason for this change is a continuing decrease in the use of traditional cameras and duplicating films throughout this sector, as more efficient scanners and other desk-top publishing products are now being used.
But graphic arts is the smallest segment sector within the photographic industry in terms of silver usage, accounting for about 34 million ounces of silver last year.
New photographic products such as the Advanced Photo System (APS) are continuing to fall behind original projections for demand though, especially in Europe and the U.S., Krause said.
The APS, including the new single-use camera, is based on a new, smaller film format which uses about one third less silver than the traditional 35mm film.
Although the system has been relaunched in the U.S., it continues to be hampered by inconsistent dealer support and poor, but expensive, photofinishing services, Krause said.
"Projections for this year put the APS market share at about five pct in the U.S., less than people hoped," Krause said in an interview with Reuters.
The other threat to photographic silver demand comes from the advent of digital photography which is making inroads into the commercial photography market.

"Here the introduction of more than 100 electronic still cameras by some 30 companies during the past 12 months, combined with a range of materials for printing digitized images, has caused marked confusion and intense competition," he said.

"Digital photography is being used by television and photo journalists where processing speed is essential, and you can buy a digital camera for about $200 now, but it doesnt take very good pictures," Krause said.
"It's estimated about 600,000-700,000 digital cameras will be sold in U.S. this year and the total number in the market is probably around 15 million compared to 800 million 35mm cameras," he said.
Kodak and Fuji have taken steps to develop hybrid systems which combine the benefits of silver halide photography with the ease of digital imagery, Krause noted.
Kodak's new "Picture Network" will enable consumers to log onto the Internet to view their photos, order reprints and e-mail pictures around the world.
Fuji's Digital Imaging Service will use the Internet to link consumers with photofinishers and retailers.
Photography is among the main uses of silver, along with jewelry, silverware and industrial applications.
In 1996 the use of silver for photography increased by about 1.4 percent to reach 226 million ounces, according to the Silver Institute.
The Silver Institute is a Washington DC based association of miners, refiners and manufacturers of silver and silver products.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
